title: Find the middle element of a linked list (slow/fast pointer).
shortTitle: Find the Middle Element of a Linked List: Slow/Fast Pointer
keyPoints: Slow pointer moves one node, fast pointer moves two; when fast finishes, slow is at the middle.
For odd-length lists, slow lands on the single middle; for even-length lists, it lands on the second of the two middles.
The loop guard `fast != null && fast.next != null` prevents null-pointer exceptions.
To land on the first of two middles for even lists, start fast at head.next instead.
The technique runs in O(n) time and O(1) space in a single pass, without counting the length.
This same skeleton underlies cycle detection, palindrome check, and list splitting.

s1_definition.oneliner: Move one pointer by one and another by two; when the fast one finishes, the slow one is at the middle.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Fast-slow pointer** – a technique where two pointers traverse at different speeds to find positional information.
- **Slow pointer** – advances one node per iteration.
- **Fast pointer** – advances two nodes per iteration.
- **Termination** – when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space, single pass without counting length.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh stores a chain of transaction nodes and wants the middle transaction for a quick spot-check. He walks two fingers along the chain: one steps on every node, the other skips every other node. When the fast finger runs off the end, the slow finger is sitting right in the middle.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
List: 100 -> 200 -> 300 -> 400 -> 500

Start:     slow = 100, fast = 100
Iteration 1: slow = 200, fast = 300
Iteration 2: slow = 300, fast = 500
             fast.next = null -> STOP

Middle = slow = 300
```

```text
List: 100 -> 200 -> 300 -> 400

Start:     slow = 100, fast = 100
Iteration 1: slow = 200, fast = 300
Iteration 2: slow = 300, fast = null
             fast = null -> STOP

Middle = slow = 300 (second of two middles)
```

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        Fast-Slow Middle Finding Flow          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                              │
│   slow = head, fast = head                   │
│       │                                      │
│       ▼                                      │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────┐         │
│   │ While fast != null             │         │
│   │    AND fast.next != null:      │         │
│   │   slow = slow.next    (+1)     │         │
│   │   fast = fast.next.next (+2)   │         │
│   └────────────────────────────────┘         │
│       │                                      │
│       ▼                                      │
│   return slow (the middle node)              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the middle of a singly linked list is the classic fast-and-slow pointer problem. Start both pointers at the head, advance slow one node and fast two nodes on each iteration. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle, done in a single pass without counting the length.

The guard condition `fast != null && fast.next != null` prevents null-pointer exceptions. The order matters: check fast first because if fast is null, accessing fast.next would crash. With this formulation, slow lands on the single middle of odd-length lists and on the second of two middles for even-length lists.

At the National Bank of India, the audit tool needed the middle transaction from a chain as a quick sampling point. The length was unknown at call time, so the single-pass fast-slow approach avoided a wasted counting pass over a long chain.

The senior-level insight is that this same skeleton underlies cycle detection, palindrome checking, and list splitting for merge sort. Recognizing the pattern across problems is the real skill.

Remember one sentence: move slow by one and fast by two; when fast finishes, slow is at the middle.
